title: Russia Restocks its Hostage Bank
content:
The main Russian security service, the FSB, arrested a foreign reporter on suspicion of espionage — this time a journalist for the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun in the Far Eastern Sakhalin region.

The incident is the latest addition to what some journalists-in-exile refer to as the Kremlin’s exchange fund. Others in the West term it a hostage bank of Westerners visiting Russia who are plucked by the FSB as a means to apply duress on their governments.

Thirty-four-year-old Yuki Imai looked bewildered and shocked as several masked FSB operatives stormed his hotel room in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the Pacific island of Sakhalin in Russia’s Far East, and threw him half-naked onto the floor. The FSB brazenly advertised its visible brutality with a video showing his arrest.

The Japanese journalist was then put on a plane bound for Moscow, and upon landing immediately taken to a Moscow court, which ruled that he should be sent to Lefortovo — the notorious FSB prison — and kept in a cell until December 12.

title: Burnham’s Big Test: Sparking a British Tech Revolution
content:
It’s a dispiriting and familiar pattern: Britain comes up with world-class ideas and startups, only to see them sold off, moved abroad, or left without the capital to pursue pilot production, customers, and manufacturing. 

Prime Minister Burnham wants to change this cycle. In his first speeches as UK leader, he outlined ambitious plans to reindustrialize, emphasizing artificial intelligence, chips, and drones. The targets are spot on. But the unanswered question is whether Burnham can turn good ideas into concrete outcomes.

Success will require close cooperation with European and American allies, encouraging foreign investment, and linking with Western supply chains. Scarce public funds should be invested in Cambridge and other existing successful tech clusters. Public procurement, particularly defense, should create credible lead customers. Private capital must be mobilized from pension funds and the country’s strong aviation companies.

title: Art Can Tell Ukraine’s Truth, Says Oscar Winner Chernov
content:
Speaking after receiving a Freedom Fighter Award from the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Chernov, who won an Oscar for 20 days in Mariupol, said there would be an intense battle to tell the story of the war and the truth must prevail.

“It is challenging to talk about the importance of art or cinema because we have very limited power to change the events; we cannot stop missiles, we cannot stop bullets,” he said. “What art can do, what cinema can do, is to defend the truth because when the war is over, and every war someday will be over, another battle will start, the battle for truth, the battle for justice.”

Speaking in a message recorded on the frontline in Ukraine and played to a CEPA Honors Gala in Washington, Chernov said he and other filmmakers, artists and journalists will try to ensure everyone knows the facts about the war, which started in 2014 and was stepped up by Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

“We will keep on going,” he said. “We will keep working, and hopefully we will all be alive.”

title: ‘Do the Right Thing’ for Ukraine, Says CEPA Award Winner Jim Berlin
content:
Berlin, who is a member of the G7 Business Advisory Council for Ukraine, said he expected others to follow his company’s lead when it stepped up to provide logistics support to the Ukrainian people after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion.

“You do the right thing hoping others will follow and honestly in this case no one did,” he said after describing deliveries of critical shipments under Russian attack. “We thought that by doing that, delivering this and letting people know, others would follow, but in truth it got much tougher.”

Logistics Plus, a shipping, warehousing and logistics company which operates in 55 countries around the world, expanded its operations in Ukraine after tanks rolled across the border in 2022. It bought another logistics company in Kyiv and opened an office in the Black Sea port of Odesa, Berlin said.

“From day one we were finding ways to get medical supplies, humanitarian goods, Starlinks, anything that’s needed over there,” he told an audience in Washington after receiving a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

title: US and Europe Tied by Mutual Dependence, Says Finland’s Stubb
content:
Dependencies between the allies are growing despite political differences, Stubb said after receiving a Global Impact Award from the Center for European Policy Analysis.

Setting out a view of geopolitics shaped by dependencies, Stubb referenced the deal he signed with President Donald Trump in October 2025 for Finland to provide ice-breakers to help the US challenge Russia and China in the high north.

“When you look at strategic dependencies around the world, you have three things you need to keep in mind,” he said. “The defensive stuff are things where you understand that you have a reliance on someone else, say, for instance, critical minerals or software and computers.”

He then discussed “offensive dependencies,” which include “things that others are dependent on you for, for instance in the Finnish case icebreakers, or data, or critical minerals or quantum.”
snippet: Dependencies between the allies are growing despite political differences, Stubb said after receiving a Global Impact Award from the Center for European Policy Analysis.
creator: Sara George

title: Washington Could Defuse Europe’s “Kill Switch” Fears
content:
When the US Commerce department issued a directive requiring AI leader Anthropic to cut access to its Fable and Mythos models for all foreign nationals, Europeans feared the worst about Washington’s power to fire a “kill switch.” 

In reality, their fears were overblown. The shutoff represented a kneejerk response to an alleged jailbreak, using the only tool available to the administration: export controls. If the White House wanted to coerce its allies, it has other, less self-destructive ways to do so than ordering its most profitable companies to shut off their services. 

Despite this, a counterproductive kill switch meme drives European policy debate. US policy that imposed export controls on AI chips under both the Biden and Trump administrations has fueled support to de-risk from the US. Europe’s kill switch fear jeopardizes Washington’s vision of a US-led global AI stack to counter China. The US could and should reassure Europeans by guaranteeing access to US AI technology.

title: Ukraine Has Problems With Both Koreas
content:
When South Korean President Lee Jae-myung lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over a prisoner-of-war transfer in September, the reaction blindsided many and raised questions about why Seoul was escalating what seemed like a relatively minor diplomatic dispute.

Ukraine had captured the two North Korean soldiers fighting for Russia, and both reportedly wanted to go to South Korea. Kyiv eventually transferred them to Seoul, but when Zelenskyy mentioned the transfer during his speech at the United Nations, Lee publicly objected.

South Korea said the transfer was supposed to remain secret, while Ukraine said there was no nondisclosure agreement. Lee accused Kyiv of effectively “branding the head of state of the other country a liar” and warned that South Korea could take additional measures against Ukraine. Seoul did not let the matter drop. It recalled its ambassador from Kyiv.

No doubt Zelenskyy’s revelation was embarrassing to the South Koreans (the news provoked some criticism inside the country for a supposed appeasement of North Korea), but the reaction seemed overblown.

title: Europe Can Rearm Even as Steel Industry Shrinks
content:
Total defense spending by EU states reached €418bn in 2025 (about $468bn), according to the European Defence Agency. Crude steel production fell to 125.8m tonnes, its lowest recorded level, says the industry association. Governments are asking arms manufacturers to expand while much of their industrial base struggles to remain profitable. This can be managed, but it requires some thought and care.

A construction-steel mill cannot simply switch to armor plate. Gun barrels require specialized metallurgy followed by advanced forging and machining. Naval components introduce different constraints, including the size of available equipment. ArcelorMittal’s specialist steel subsidiary Industeel uses vacuum treatment and controlled plate production for protection steels. Comparable chemistry alone does not make another supplier acceptable. Qualification takes time, and an idle furnace cannot clear a queue at a heat-treatment line.

title: Ukraine’s Military Recruitment: Lessons for NATO
content:
NATO’s armies are facing manpower challenges in peacetime, but Ukraine is managing to strengthen and reform its armed forces even while it is defending a 1,200 km (750-mile) frontline in an unrelenting war.

Replenishing troop numbers is one of Kyiv’s most critical challenges, especially given Russia’s numeric advantage and its sourcing of troops from abroad. The current strength of the Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel is estimated at 880,000–900,000, compared with an authorized strength of 1.55 million personnel in the Russian Armed Forces.

Ukraine is changing its approach to manning the military. A decentralized recruitment system aimed at attracting motivated volunteers has been developed since 2024. In May 2026, Kyiv announced the first phase of military reforms, which are expected to increase the number of people willing to join the armed forces.

Mobilization, which remains the cornerstone of personnel replenishment, has faced a number of challenges. Natural fatigue and the intensity of hostilities have contributed to a rise in cases of draft evasion and unauthorized absence, placing additional pressure on units already operating under extremely difficult conditions.

title: The Anxiety Machine
content:
AI poses an existential risk to humanity. Or it will destroy all jobs. Or it will go rogue and escape control. These are headlines in reputable news outlets, but they are wrong. The mechanism that creates these concerns is a media that amplifies the fears and hostility of a class of public intellectuals and then disseminates them to an already anxious public. In some cases, AI anxiety serves the unstated financial interests of particular individuals or groups — Russia and China, for example, may try to expand these narratives — but there is usually an element of truth behind the fears, which means they cannot be immediately dismissed.

For AI, risks remain hypothetical. No one has connected the dots that show how you get from superintelligence or Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) to an existential threat. The absence of practical detail makes it likely that an existential AI threat is both hypothetical and improbable.

title: Readying the Nordics for War – Let’s Not Waste Time
content:
The Russian threat rises and rises. The risks and costs from its shadow (and sometimes open) attacks are increasing, and at some point soon there will be a serious crisis, perhaps brought on by the casualties from a successful version of the Kremlin’s bungled strike at Leipzig Airport in August.

Facing this, Europe’s most aware and best-prepared countries are represented by the Baltic states and the Nordic nations of Norway, Denmark, Sweden and Finland. They have been spending and reorganizing at speed since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, as has Germany.

With France and the UK, the continent’s traditional security heavyweights, hamstrung by enormous debt loads and seemingly unable to make decisive increases in defense spending, and the US now focused elsewhere, the Nordic countries cannot expect others to provide leadership.

They should take the next step toward a unified fighting system. Major work is already underway. Nordic troops are now in Finland, as well as the Baltics, while the Nordic Airpower Concept (NAPC), which offers a unified command over more than 250 modern combat aircraft, started operations early last year.

title: Putin and Xi United by a Love of Corruption
content:
Countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia are among the world’s worst for corruption, with widespread impunity driven by the vested interests that dominate many of their governments.

Western European nations fill nine places in the list of the best 10 countries globally in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI), but the continent’s anti-corruption efforts have largely stalled in recent years, with the region’s average CPI score dropping quicker than in any other region.

Of the 182 countries ranked in the latest CPI, published in February, the top ranks included Denmark in first place, with Finland and Singapore second and third, while those perceived as the most corrupt included Venezuela at 180th and South Sudan and Somalia tied at 181st.
snippet: Countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia are among the world’s worst for corruption, with widespread impunity driven by the vested interests that dominate many of their governments.

title: Trust Is as Important to NATO as Guns
content:
The alliance cannot sustain collective defense if its citizens doubt why it exists, distrust what it says, or come to believe it is responsible for the threats it confronts. Public trust in NATO should be seen as a key part of Europe’s security infrastructure.

Societal trust is crucial to countering Russia in the information sphere, which is where the narrative battles take place. For NATO members, these battles matter because public acceptance of Moscow’s false claim that the West caused the war could weaken support for Ukraine and for the alliance’s broader deterrence mission.

Polling in all 32 NATO member states suggests this matters. In a survey conducted across the alliance, respondents who trusted NATO were far more likely to blame Russia for starting the war; people with greater faith in the alliance were nearly three times more likely to blame Russia and had about 65% lower odds of blaming the West and Ukraine, compared to those who did not.

The results revealed that distrust in supranational and alliance institutions is strongly associated with West blame.
